For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

The age-old debate about wedding registries. I'm happy to help you navigate this situation. Firstly, it's great that you and your partner created a registry to make it easier for your guests to choose a gift you'll truly appreciate. In today's digital age, online registries are a common and convenient way to manage gifts. Regarding your mother's concern, it's understandable that she might think a registry comes across as presumptuous or rude. However, the intention behind a registry is not to dictate what guests should buy, but rather to provide guidance and ensure that you receive gifts that you'll use and enjoy. Here are a few points to consider: 1. **Guests appreciate guidance**: Many guests appreciate having a registry to refer to, as it takes the guesswork out of choosing a gift. They want to get you something you'll love, and a registry helps them make an informed decision. 2. **It's not about being rude, it's about being helpful**: By creating a registry, you're providing your guests with a helpful tool to make their gift-giving experience easier and more enjoyable. 3. **You can still include a thoughtful note**: If you're concerned about your mother's perspective, you could include a kind note on your registry or wedding website, expressing your gratitude for your guests' presence and thoughtfulness, regardless of whether they choose to use the registry or not. Ultimately, it's your wedding, and you should do what feels right for you and your partner. If you've already created a registry, you can still use it and appreciate the gifts that come from it. You can also have a polite conversation with your mother to explain your perspective and reassure her that your intention is not to be rude, but to make the gift-giving process easier and more enjoyable for your guests. I hope this helps, and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!

AITA for expecting family time? | This morning I woke up and saw my husband watching video game streams, his typical pastime. Later he said the streamers he was watching were having cash giveaways that required participation to be entered. He continued to watch while he covertly built the kids' bikes in the garage as I had asked, then left to run a last-minute grocery errand for dinner, then came home and went upstairs to watch more streaming. After wrapping gifts, I did dishes and put dinner in the oven, and asked him to turn it off to spend time with me with/without kids. He said no. That the stream was only for today and it is not okay for me to expect him to stop doing what he finds enjoyable just because I want him to do something I find enjoyable. But if I was okay letting him spend $100 on app purchases for this game (same one he's watching) that he'd shut it off no problem. But last year he spent a little over $2,000 on in-app purchases for this game, and after a lengthy discussion, said he wouldn't buy anymore. So I'm not a huge fan of okaying any more money for it. It's almost 6pm and says he doesn't know when it will end, but that there are 2 more streamers left. I feel like the evening is almost over and I am so disappointed and feel saddened that he would rather watch games than spend time with me. Am I an asshole for being upset and having unrealistic expectations?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I would answer: 0 (NTA - Not The Asshole) Here's why: 1. **You asked him to spend time with you**: You made a reasonable request to spend time with your husband, which is a normal expectation in a relationship. You didn't demand that he drop everything, but rather asked him to take a break from his streaming to engage with you and possibly the kids. 2. **He prioritized his hobby over family time**: Your husband chose to continue watching streams, even after you asked him to stop, and instead offered a condition (spending $100 on in-app purchases) for him to spend time with you. This implies that his hobby takes precedence over your request for quality time together. 3. **He has a history of excessive spending on the game**: The fact that he spent over $2,000 on in-app purchases last year and is now asking you to okay more spending raises concerns about his priorities and responsibility. It's reasonable that you wouldn't want to enable further excessive spending. 4. **You've contributed to the household**: You mentioned doing dishes, putting dinner in the oven, and wrapping gifts, which suggests that you've been contributing to the household and taking care of responsibilities. It's not unfair to expect your partner to reciprocate and spend time with you. 5. **His response was conditional and dismissive**: Your husband's response came across as dismissive of your feelings and expectations. He implied that you're being unreasonable for expecting him to stop watching streams, and instead offered a condition that you're not comfortable with. Overall, it's not unreasonable to expect your partner to prioritize family time and engage with you, especially when you've made a reasonable request. Your husband's response and behavior suggest that he's prioritizing his hobby over your relationship, which is a legitimate concern.
